entities.summary:
Cynaegirus, an Athenian hoplite and brother of the celebrated tragedian Aeschylus, emerged as a potent symbol of Hellenic defiance against the Achaemenid Persian Empire during the crucial Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE. His desperate, ultimately fatal, act of valor in attempting to prevent Persian ships from retreating cemented his place in the historical memory of Classical Athens as an embodiment of patriotic sacrifice, contributing to the nascent Greek self-identity forged in the crucible of the Persian Wars. Born around 600 BCE into an aristocratic family, his death in 490 BCE marked the culmination of a life dedicated to Athenian civic and military service, elevating him to a legendary status that transcended his individual actions.

The defining moment of Cynaegirus's life occurred on the plains of Marathon, approximately 42 kilometers northeast of Athens, in September 490 BCE. As the vastly outnumbered Athenian and Plataean forces routed the Persian infantry, Cynaegirus, according to accounts by historians such as Herodotus and later elaborated by Plutarch and Justin, pursued the fleeing Persians to their ships. In a legendary display of zeal, he seized the stern of a Persian trireme, attempting to hold it back from escaping the beach. During this desperate struggle, a Persian axe-man severed his hand, causing him to fall into the sea, where he drowned or bled to death. This act, though failing to prevent the ships' full departure, became a vivid testament to Athenian determination and martial spirit.
